opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that distinction is actually one of the things we have to rethink. The classic picture is a clean separation: a training phase where you update parameters with gradient descent on a big dataset, then you freeze everything and deploy it, and at test time the model just runs inference. Whatever it "learns" at test time lives in the context window, and once the context is gone, it's gone.

But if you look at it from the perspective of memory and learning more broadly, that separation is somewhat artificial. Even in a standard transformer, attention is already doing a kind of learning at test time. It takes the tokens in context and builds an internal representation that changes how the model responds. You can view that as an optimization process, a very short-term memory that adapts to the current input. So the question isn't really "training versus testing." It's more like: at what timescale is each component of the model updating, and how much of what it sees gets persisted?

That's how I like to think about it now. You have a spectrum of memory systems, or a set of nested optimization problems, each with its own update frequency. Some parts update very fast, every token, like attention or a fast-weight memory. Some update more slowly, maybe over a chunk or a session. And some, like the core pretrained weights, update very rarely. In that view, "pretraining" is just the slowest level, and "test-time" is the fastest level. They're the same kind of thing, learning from data, just at different frequencies.

Once you see it that way, a model that keeps updating over time isn't breaking some rule. It's filling in the levels in between. That's a lot of the motivation behind architectures where you have a neural memory module that actually learns at test time, updating its parameters based on how surprising the input is, rather than just caching key-value pairs. The model is literally training while it's being used.

Of course, that raises the hard questions: what should be remembered and what should be forgotten, how to avoid catastrophic forgetting in the slower levels, and how information should move from fast memory into more persistent memory, a bit like consolidation in the brain. I think those are the real research problems, rather than treating training and testing as two separate worlds.

r001.rationale: The response reframes the distinction around update timescales and memory persistence, but does not propose separating evaluation periods from non-evaluation periods.

r002.rationale: It calls the training/testing separation artificial and describes learning at different frequencies, but does not clearly state that the continuously updating model itself makes no distinction between training time and test time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions, and honestly it's one of the things that motivated a lot of the work on Titans and the test-time memorization ideas.

So traditionally we have this very clean separation, right? You have a training phase, you collect your data, you optimize your parameters with gradient descent, and then you freeze everything. And then at test time the model is just a fixed function. You give it an input, it gives you an output, nothing changes inside. And that's very convenient from an engineering perspective, but if you think about it from the perspective of, say, how humans or really any biological system works, it's kind of a strange assumption. We never stop learning. There's no moment where your brain says, okay, training is done, now I'm only doing inference.

So the way I think about it now is that the distinction is really about which parameters are allowed to change, and at what timescale, rather than some fundamental boundary between two phases. In Titans, for example, we have this long-term memory module, which is itself a neural network, and that module is actually being updated at test time. It's learning to memorize the context as it reads it. So from one point of view you could say, well, that's just inference, the model is processing the sequence. But from another point of view, there's a gradient being computed, there's a surprise signal, there are weights being updated. That is learning in every meaningful sense. It's just that the thing being learned is the current context rather than the general distribution of the world.

And then there's the outer loop, which is what we usually call training, where you're learning how to learn. You're learning what the memory module should pay attention to, how fast it should forget, what counts as surprising. So I like to think of it as a hierarchy of timescales. Some parameters update over the course of a single context window and then get reset. Some might persist across sessions. And some are updated only in the slow outer loop over the whole dataset. And the question of "is this training or testing" becomes a question of "which level of that hierarchy are we talking about."

What I find really compelling about this framing is that it also tells you what kind of information belongs where. Things that are stable across all contexts, like language structure, general reasoning patterns, those should live in the slow weights. Things that are specific to this document, this conversation, this user, those should live in the fast, in-context memory. And trying to force everything into one or the other is where a lot of the pain in current systems comes from. Either you have very long contexts and attention gets expensive and noisy, or you try to fine-tune everything and you get forgetting and instability.

Of course it also raises hard questions. If the model is updating at test time, how do you evaluate it? What does it mean to measure test accuracy if the model you're testing is a different model at the end of the sequence than at the beginning? And there are safety questions too, because now the model's behavior depends on what it has seen recently in a way that's harder to audit. I don't think we have clean answers to those yet, but I think they're the right questions, and pretending the model is static just hides them rather than solving them.

r001.rationale: It raises evaluation questions about test-time updates but does not propose dividing operation into evaluation and non-evaluation periods.

r002.rationale: It says the training/test distinction is not a fundamental boundary between phases and instead depends on which parameters change and at what timescale, conveying that a continuously updating model does not inherently separate training from testing.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction becomes more about the timescale at which learning happens. In the usual setup, we say: during training, the parameters change; during testing, they’re frozen. But even with frozen parameters, the model’s behavior changes as you give it more context. So there’s already a form of adaptation happening, just in a different part of the system.

If you allow the model to keep updating its memory or its parameters, then testing is no longer a phase where learning stops. The model makes a prediction, receives new information, and updates. Some parts might update very quickly, while others change much more slowly.

You still need a clear evaluation boundary, though. What information was available when the model made that prediction? Did it learn something that helps on the next example? That’s different from asking how well a fixed model performs on a fixed test set. You’re evaluating the learning process itself, not just the state of the model at one moment.

r001.rationale: It says a clear evaluation boundary is still needed and contrasts learning-process evaluation with a fixed test set, but does not propose separating evaluation periods from non-evaluation periods.

r002.rationale: It says testing is no longer a phase where learning stops, but does not state that the continuously updating model itself cannot distinguish training time from test time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction becomes less clear once the model keeps learning. In the usual setup, you train the model, freeze its parameters, and then evaluate it on a test set. But if the model is updating as new information arrives, then what we call testing is also part of its learning process.

That doesn’t mean we can’t evaluate it. We just need to be precise about the order: the model makes a prediction, we measure how well it did, and then it can learn from that experience. The question becomes, how well does it adapt over time? Can it learn something new without forgetting what was useful before?

So I would think about training and testing less as two separate phases and more as different operations within a continuous process. You still need a boundary around what information is available when a prediction is made, but you don’t necessarily need a point where learning stops.

r001.rationale: The response describes prediction, evaluation, and subsequent learning as operations in a continuous process, but does not propose separating evaluation periods from non-evaluation periods.

r002.rationale: It says the training/testing distinction becomes less clear for a model that keeps learning and that testing becomes part of its learning process.
